\chapter{Pinning Down Which One}
\label{ch:cada-y-mismo}
\hlchaptermodality{345}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say mismo, cada, la parte, la persona and el objeto, and say why a Latin actor's mask became the ordinary word for a human being.}

Complete ES-C345-objeto: say it is the same one, take a set one at a time, name a share of it, name a single human being, and name a thing on purpose.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mismo]{mismo — the very same, from a word built by piling on emphasis}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-mismo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the dozen}, then \emph{double}. (\emph{La docena}; \emph{doble}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item otro — the word this answers.
  \item todo — another of the pointing words.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MIS-mo}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{s} stays clean and never buzzes into a \emph{z}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mismo} — \textquotedblleft{}same,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}very,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}self.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had \textbf{ipse}, \emph{self, the very one}. Spoken Latin decided that was not emphatic enough, and started stacking.

First \textbf{met}, an emphasising particle, was stuck on the front: \emph{egomet}, \emph{I myself}. Then the superlative ending \emph{-issimus} was piled on the back. The result was something like \textbf{metipsimus} — roughly \emph{the very most self-est one}, a word made almost entirely of insistence.

That collapsed into Spanish \textbf{mismo}, French \emph{même} and Italian \emph{medesimo}. All three languages built their ordinary word for \emph{same} out of somebody thumping a fist on the bar.

English kept \emph{ipse} undisguised in a few borrowed phrases. \textbf{Ipso facto} is \emph{by that very fact}. \textbf{Solipsism} is \emph{self-alone-ism}, the belief that only oneself exists. And \textbf{ipsissima verba} are \emph{the very words themselves}.

Spanish uses \emph{mismo} both ways: \textbf{el mismo libro} is \emph{the same book}, and \textbf{yo mismo} is \emph{I myself}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first word for pinning down which one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mismo}
  \item \emph{el mismo libro}
  \item \emph{yo mismo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Latin word is under \emph{mismo}? (\emph{Ipse}, self.) And what does \emph{ipso facto} mean? (By that very fact.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cada]{cada — each, one by one, and a Greek word in plain clothes}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-cada}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{double}, then \emph{same, self}. (\emph{Doble}; \emph{mismo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item todo — the whole this divides.
  \item mismo — the other pinning word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KA-da}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{d} between vowels is soft, close to the \emph{th} in \emph{this}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{cada} — \textquotedblleft{}each,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}every.\textquotedblright{}

A very small, very common word, and it is Greek.

Greek \textbf{katá} meant \emph{down, along, by}. It entered late spoken Latin in the phrase \textbf{cata ūnum} — \emph{one by one} — which is exactly the sense \emph{cada} still carries: not the whole heap at once, but taken one at a time.

That is the difference between \emph{cada} and \textbf{todo}, which you have. \emph{Todo} is the whole thing together; \emph{cada} walks through it item by item.

Greek \emph{katá} is at the front of a row of English words. A \textbf{catalogue} lists things down the page. A \textbf{catastrophe} is a \emph{down-turning}, the moment a play overturns. A \textbf{cathedral} is where a bishop sits \textbf{down}. \textbf{Catalyst}, \textbf{category} and \textbf{catapult} all start the same way.

So the everyday \textbf{cada día}, \emph{each day}, opens with the same syllable as \emph{catastrophe}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Wholes can now be walked through one at a time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cada}
  \item \emph{cada día}
  \item \emph{cada libro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which language does \emph{cada} come from? (Greek — \emph{katá}.) And what is a \emph{catastrophe}, word for word? (A down-turning.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la parte]{la parte — the part, and why a party is only a portion of the people}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-parte}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{same, self}, then \emph{each, every}. (\emph{Mismo}; \emph{cada}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la mitad — one particular part.
  \item todo — what parts are taken from.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PAR-te}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} is a single tap, never a full trill here. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la parte} — \textquotedblleft{}the part,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the share.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pars}, accusative \textbf{partem}, meant \emph{a part, a portion, a share}.

English took it and then took it again, and again, until it had a whole shelf. A \textbf{part} is a piece. Something \textbf{partial} covers only some of it. A \textbf{particle} is a very small piece. To \textbf{participate} is to take a part. A \textbf{partner} is one who shares a part with you. A \textbf{portion} is a serving. And a \textbf{party} is a \emph{part} of the people, taken apart from the rest — which is as true of a political party as of a dinner one.

Spanish uses it where English often reaches for a different word entirely. \textbf{¿De parte de quién?} is what somebody says when answering a telephone — \emph{on whose part?}, meaning \emph{who is calling?} And \textbf{en parte} means \emph{partly}.

Beside \emph{la mitad}, which is a half exactly, \emph{la parte} is any share at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Shares of a thing, not merely halves of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la parte}
  \item \emph{una parte}
  \item \emph{en parte}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{partem} mean? (A part, a share.) And what is a \emph{party}, word for word? (A part of the people, taken apart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la persona]{la persona — the person, who began as a mask}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-persona}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{each, every}, then \emph{the part}. (\emph{Cada}; \emph{la parte}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la gente — people in the mass, not one by one.
  \item cada — how you take them one at a time.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{per-SO-na}, three beats with the weight on the middle. The \emph{r} is a single tap, and the \emph{s} stays clean. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la persona} — \textquotedblleft{}the person.\textquotedblright{}

In Latin, a \textbf{persōna} was not a human being. It was \emph{a mask} — the carved face a Roman actor held up or wore on stage. Probably from Etruscan, and often explained as \emph{per-sonāre}, \emph{to sound through}, because the mask's mouth carried the voice.

From the mask came the part the actor played, and from the part came the human being playing it. So the ordinary word for a human being started life as the thing worn over a human face.

The mask is still visible in English. Your \textbf{personality} is the face you show. A \textbf{persona} is a mask you adopt on purpose. To \textbf{impersonate} is to put on somebody else's. Something \textbf{personal} belongs behind the mask.

Even grammar keeps it: the first, second and third \textbf{person} are the three masks a speaker can wear — \emph{I}, \emph{you}, and \emph{the one being talked about}.

Beside \textbf{la gente}, which is people in the mass, \emph{la persona} is one at a time.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
People one at a time, with a mask underneath the word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la persona}
  \item \emph{una persona}
  \item \emph{cada persona}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{persōna} in Latin? (An actor's mask.) And what are the three grammatical \emph{persons}? (The three masks a speaker can wear.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el objeto]{el objeto — the object, thrown down in front of you}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-objeto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the part}, then \emph{the person}. (\emph{La parte}; \emph{la persona}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cosa — the everyday word beside this one.
  \item la parte — another of the pinning words.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ob-HE-to}, three beats with the weight on the middle. The \emph{j} is the throaty \emph{jota}, and the \emph{b} is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el objeto} — \textquotedblleft{}the object,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the thing.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{iacere} meant \emph{to throw}. Add \textbf{ob-}, \emph{before, against}, and you get \textbf{objectum} — \emph{the thing thrown down in front of you}. An object is whatever has been put in your way to be considered.

\emph{Iacere} is one of the great English factories, and every one of its children is a throw. To \textbf{project} is to throw forward. To \textbf{inject} is to throw in. To \textbf{eject} is to throw out. To \textbf{reject} is to throw back. To \textbf{subject} somebody is to throw them under. To \textbf{interject} is to throw a remark between. A \textbf{trajectory} is the path of a throw. And to \textbf{object} to something is to throw it in the other person's path.

Spanish has both \textbf{la cosa}, which is the everyday word for a thing, and \textbf{el objeto}, which is the deliberate one — the thing considered, the thing put in front of you on purpose.

That closes the set: \emph{mismo}, \emph{cada}, \emph{la parte}, \emph{la persona}, \emph{el objeto}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words for pinning down which one, and the tranche is closed: thirty words across six chapters.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el objeto}
  \item \emph{un objeto}
  \item \emph{el mismo objeto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{iacere} mean? (To throw.) And what is a \emph{projectile}, word for word? (A thing thrown forward.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — the mask, the share, and the thing thrown down}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-repaso-persona-objeto}



\begin{quote}
Two nouns from this chapter. The person. (\emph{La persona}.) The object. (\emph{El objeto}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three chants, and one thing they share.

\textbf{First.} \emph{La parte.} — Latin \emph{partem}: a piece cut off a whole.

\textbf{Second.} \emph{La persona.} — Latin \emph{persōna}: a carved \textbf{mask}, held up in front of an actor's face.

\textbf{Third.} \emph{El objeto.} — Latin \emph{objectum}: something \textbf{thrown down in front of} you.

Every one of those started as a thing you could pick up. A cut piece. A mask. A thrown thing. And every one of them now names something with no shape at all — a share, a human being, a topic.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Here is the part worth keeping, and it is not about vocabulary.

You did not meet \emph{persona} and \emph{objeto} this chapter. You have been using both for three hundred chapters, as \textbf{grammar labels}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{primera} \emph{\textbf{persona}} — first person: \emph{hablo}. \emph{\textbf{objeto}} \emph{directo} — direct object: \emph{lo tengo}.
\end{quote}

The first, second and third \textbf{person} are three masks a speaker can wear: \emph{I}, \emph{you}, and the one being talked about. And the \textbf{object} of a verb is exactly what the word says — the thing the action is thrown at.

So the grammar words were never jargon. They were ordinary Spanish nouns the whole time, doing the same job in a classroom that they do in a kitchen.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la parte}, \emph{la persona}, \emph{el objeto}
  \item \emph{primera persona}, then \emph{objeto directo} — the same two words, at work
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{objeto} mean before it meant a thing? (Something \textbf{thrown down in front of} you.) And where had you already been using \emph{persona} without noticing? (In \emph{primera persona} — the grammar label.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — three plain words, none of them one piece}

\label{lesson:ES-C345-repaso-cada-mismo-objeto}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Same.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Mismo}.) \textquotedblleft{}Each.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Cada}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of this chapter's words lean on a noun to say \textbf{which one}, and the chapter gave you the plainest noun there is to lean them on.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Cada \textbf{objeto}.} — each object. \emph{El mismo \textbf{objeto}.} — the same object.
\end{quote}

Say both and the difference is doing real work: \emph{cada} takes them one at a time, \emph{mismo} says this one is the one you already met.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now look underneath. Not one of the three is a single piece.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{mismo}} was \emph{ipse}, \textquotedblleft{}self\textquotedblright{}, with emphasis piled on it until it meant the very selfsame one. English keeps \emph{ipse} bare in \emph{ipso facto}.
  \item \emph{\textbf{cada}} is Greek \emph{kata}, \textquotedblleft{}down, by\textquotedblright{}, which reached Latin in the phrase \emph{cata unum} — \textbf{one by one}, which is exactly what \emph{cada} still does. English keeps \emph{kata} at the front of \emph{catalogue} and \emph{cathedral}.
  \item \emph{\textbf{objeto}} is \emph{ob} plus \emph{iacere}, thrown before. English \emph{project} throws forward, \emph{inject} throws in, \emph{eject} throws out.
\end{itemize}

Three of the most ordinary words in the chapter, and each is a small machine with the parts still visible — in Spanish, and in English too.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{cada objeto}, \emph{el mismo objeto} — the noun steady, the word in front doing the choosing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word takes them one at a time? (\emph{\textbf{Cada}}.) And what was \emph{el objeto} before it was a thing? (Something \textbf{thrown down in front of} you.)
\end{tcolorbox}
